notes:
Task and constraints: `tree2str(root)` serializes a binary tree using node values and parentheses, omitting unnecessary empty child pairs while preserving a right child when present.
Idea: Handle null and leaf nodes directly, then format the left and right subtree cases separately.
Technique and why it applies: When `root.right is None`, the result includes only `({self.tree2str(root.left)})`; if a right child exists, both child strings are emitted in order so the right subtree remains distinguishable.
Invariant: Each recursive result represents exactly the subtree rooted at `root`, with child positions encoded according to the serialization rules.
Edge cases: A null root returns an empty string; a leaf returns only its value; a right child requires the left-parentheses pair even when the left child is null.
Complexity: O(n) time to visit all nodes and construct the serialization, with O(h) recursion space plus output for tree height h.
complexity_reason: The left-child parentheses cannot be omitted when a right child exists, because they preserve which side contains that subtree.

notes:
Task and constraints: `tree2str(TreeNode root)` creates the required parenthesized representation of a binary tree without redundant empty child pairs.
Idea: Return an empty string for null, the value for a leaf, and use separate formats depending on whether the right child exists.
Technique and why it applies: `tree2str(root.left)` supplies the left representation; when `root.right != null`, a second parenthesized `tree2str(root.right)` is appended, retaining the right-child position.
Invariant: Each recursive call returns a representation of precisely its input subtree, and the parent format preserves left-versus-right structure.
Edge cases: Null root returns `""`; leaves return `Integer.toString(root.val)`; a right-only node still emits empty left parentheses.
Complexity: O(n) time to process all nodes and O(h) recursion space plus output for tree height h.
complexity_reason: Including the empty left-child parentheses for a right-only node prevents its right child from being misread as a left child.

notes:
Task and constraints: `findDuplicate(paths)` groups full file paths whose file contents are identical, based on directory-description strings.
Idea: Parse each description, use `groups` to map each content to its paths, then return only groups containing multiple paths.
Technique and why it applies: `desc.split()` separates the directory from file entries; `file.split('(', 1)` separates the name and content, and `content[:-1]` removes the closing parenthesis before grouping `directory + '/' + name`.
Invariant: Every parsed file path is stored under its content key, so each returned list represents files with the same content.
Edge cases: Files with unique content are filtered out; the parsing assumes the specified format and content strings do not contain an ambiguous closing delimiter.
Complexity: O(S) time and O(S) space for total input size S, including grouped paths and keys.
complexity_reason: Filtering with `len(g) > 1` excludes content values that occur in only one file.

notes:
Task and constraints: `findDuplicate(String[] paths)` returns groups of full paths that share identical file contents.
Idea: Parse each directory description and populate `Map<String, List<String>> g`, then collect only lists with more than one path.
Technique and why it applies: `indexOf('(')` locates the filename/content boundary; `substring(at + 1, f.length() - 1)` extracts content, and `computeIfAbsent` creates its path list before adding `dir + "/" + filename`.
Invariant: Every file is assigned to the map entry for its content, and the final `out` contains only duplicate-content groups.
Edge cases: Unique contents are omitted; the code relies on the problem's parenthesized file format and whitespace-separated directory descriptions.
Complexity: O(S) time and O(S) space in the total input size S for parsing, map entries, and stored paths.
complexity_reason: A content key accumulates all paths with that exact extracted content, and only groups larger than one are returned.

notes:
Task and constraints: `triangleNumber(nums)` counts index triples whose three values can form a non-degenerate triangle.
Idea: Sort `nums`, fix the largest side at `k`, and use two pointers `i` and `j` to count valid pairs.
Technique and why it applies: If `nums[i] + nums[j] > nums[k]`, then every index from `i` through `j - 1` pairs with `j`, adding `j - i`; otherwise `i` advances to increase the sum.
Invariant: For each fixed largest side, the pointer region still contains the pairs not yet counted or ruled out.
Edge cases: Fewer than three elements yields zero; sorting mutates the input; the strict `>` enforces a non-degenerate triangle.
Complexity: O(n²) time after sorting and O(1) auxiliary space excluding sorting.
complexity_reason: Because the array is sorted, once `nums[i] + nums[j]` exceeds the largest side, every index between i and j also works with j.

notes:
Task and constraints: `triangleNumber(int[] a)` counts triples of side lengths satisfying the strict triangle inequality.
Idea: Sort `a`, choose each `a[k]` as the largest side, and scan with pointers `i` and `j`.
Technique and why it applies: When `a[i] + a[j] > a[k]`, the `j - i` pairs ending at `j` are valid; otherwise `i++` increases the smaller side.
Invariant: For a fixed `k`, each successful count adds all remaining smaller indices paired with `j`, without recounting pairs from previous pointer positions.
Edge cases: Arrays shorter than three return zero; the strict inequality excludes degenerate triangles; `Arrays.sort(a)` changes the input array.
Complexity: O(n²) time after sorting and O(1) auxiliary space excluding sort.
complexity_reason: Sorted order makes all indices from i to j minus one valid partners for j whenever the smallest candidate sum passes.

notes:
Task and constraints: `mergeTrees(a, b)` merges two binary trees by summing overlapping node values and preserving any subtree that exists on only one side.
Idea: Return the non-null tree when the other node is absent; otherwise add values and recursively merge matching child positions.
Technique and why it applies: `a.val += b.val` combines overlapping nodes, and assignments to `a.left` and `a.right` replace each child with its merged result.
Invariant: Each returned node represents the merged result for the corresponding pair of input subtrees, while non-overlapping branches are reused unchanged.
Edge cases: Two null nodes return null through the first branch; if only one node exists, its entire subtree is returned; the implementation mutates tree `a`.
Complexity: O(min(n,m)) time for overlapping node pairs plus constant handling of recursive boundaries, with O(h) recursion space.
complexity_reason: Returning the non-null argument immediately preserves its entire unmatched subtree without copying every descendant.

notes:
Task and constraints: `mergeTrees(TreeNode a, TreeNode b)` sums values where both trees have nodes and retains unmatched branches.
Idea: Return `b` if `a` is null, return `a` if `b` is null, otherwise merge values and recurse on both child pairs.
Technique and why it applies: `a.val += b.val` combines overlapping values; assignments from `mergeTrees(a.left, b.left)` and the corresponding right call attach the merged children.
Invariant: The returned node is the correct merge of the two input subtrees, with unmatched descendants preserved through direct returns.
Edge cases: If either root is null, the other tree is returned; when both are null the first branch returns null; the method mutates the first tree where nodes overlap.
Complexity: O(min(n,m)) time for overlapping nodes, with O(h) recursive stack space.
complexity_reason: The early null checks reuse a whole unmatched subtree, and overlapping nodes are updated in place.

notes:
Task and constraints: `leastInterval(tasks, n)` computes the minimum schedule length for uppercase-letter tasks with at least `n` intervals between identical tasks.
Idea: Count task frequencies, find the maximum frequency `high` and number `tied` of tasks reaching it, then take the maximum of task count and the frame lower bound.
Technique and why it applies: `(high - 1) * (n + 1) + tied` models the cooldown-separated frames for most frequent tasks, while `len(tasks)` handles schedules where other tasks fill the gaps.
Invariant: The result respects both the total number of required tasks and the minimum spacing forced by the most frequent task types.
Edge cases: With no cooldown, the task count dominates; ties for maximum frequency extend the final frame by `tied`; inputs are uppercase task labels as assumed.
Complexity: O(n_tasks) time to count tasks and O(1) space for the fixed alphabet frequency map.
complexity_reason: The frame formula is a lower bound from the most frequent tasks, while the total task count prevents unnecessary idle intervals.

notes:
Task and constraints: `leastInterval(char[] tasks, int n)` returns the minimum number of intervals needed while respecting the cooldown between equal tasks.
Idea: Count each of the 26 uppercase task frequencies, compute `high`, count how many types tie at that frequency, and apply the frame formula.
Technique and why it applies: `f[t - 'A']` indexes the alphabet array; `(high - 1) * (n + 1) + tied` captures required cooldown frames and `Math.max(tasks.length, ...)` prevents a schedule shorter than the tasks themselves.
Invariant: `high` is the maximum frequency after counting, and `tied` counts all task types with that maximum.
Edge cases: If cooldown gaps can be filled by other tasks, `tasks.length` is the answer; tied maximum-frequency tasks occupy the end of the frame.
Complexity: O(N) time for N tasks and O(1) auxiliary space for the fixed 26-entry array.
complexity_reason: The fixed alphabet array keeps counting space constant, and the maximum with task count handles fully occupied schedules.

notes:
Task and constraints: `addOneRow(root, val, depth)` inserts a row at the requested depth and attaches old subtrees to the specified new children.
Idea: For depth one, create a new root; otherwise traverse iteratively with `(node, d)` stack entries until reaching the parent depth.
Technique and why it applies: At `d == depth - 1`, the new `left` node receives `node.left` as its left child and the new `right` node receives `node.right` as its right child; the tuple stack tracks depths explicitly.
Invariant: Nodes above the insertion level retain their structure, while each node at depth `depth - 1` gets two new children that preserve its former subtrees.
Edge cases: Depth one creates a new root even if the original root is null; a null root at a deeper depth returns null; the input tree is modified in place.
Complexity: O(n) time in the worst case and O(w) explicit stack space, where w is the maximum number of queued or stacked nodes at a level.
complexity_reason: The old left subtree stays under the new left node and the old right subtree under the new right node.

notes:
Task and constraints: `addOneRow(TreeNode root, int val, int depth)` inserts nodes at a specified tree depth while preserving existing subtrees on the required sides.
Idea: Create a new root when `depth == 1`; otherwise use an `ArrayDeque` queue to advance level by level to the parent depth.
Technique and why it applies: `size = q.size()` bounds each breadth-first level; at depth `depth - 1`, new `l` and `r` nodes take `x.left` and `x.right` as their corresponding children before replacing `x.left` and `x.right`.
Invariant: Each queue iteration advances one level, and when insertion occurs each old left or right subtree remains on its same side below the new row.
Edge cases: Depth one returns a new root; null root at deeper depth returns null; the loop may finish before the requested depth if the tree is too shallow.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(w) queue space for maximum level width w, despite the supplied metadata describing traversal stack space.
complexity_reason: The breadth-first `size` snapshot ensures each loop iteration processes one depth and does not accidentally traverse newly added nodes.

notes:
Task and constraints: `maximumProduct(nums)` returns the largest product of any three elements, including cases where negative values make two small numbers useful.
Idea: Sort `nums` and compare the product of the three largest values with the product of the two smallest values and the largest value.
Technique and why it applies: `nums[-1] * nums[-2] * nums[-3]` covers three large values; `nums[0] * nums[1] * nums[-1]` covers a potentially large positive product from two negatives.
Invariant: For a sorted array, the maximum product must come from one of these two combinations of extremes.
Edge cases: At least three values are required; negative values and zeros make checking both candidates necessary; sorting mutates `nums`.
Complexity: O(n log n) time dominated by sorting and O(1) auxiliary space excluding sort.
complexity_reason: Two negative minima can multiply into a large positive value, so the largest three alone are not sufficient.

notes:
Task and constraints: `maximumProduct(int[] a)` finds the maximum product among all triples in an integer array.
Idea: Sort `a` and compare the product of its three largest values with the product of its two smallest values and largest value.
Technique and why it applies: `Math.max` selects between `a[n-1] * a[n-2] * a[n-3]` and `a[0] * a[1] * a[n-1]`, covering the main sign patterns that can maximize a triple product.
Invariant: After sorting, an optimal triple uses either the three largest values or the two most negative values with the largest value.
Edge cases: The input must contain at least three elements; negative values can make the second candidate larger; `Arrays.sort(a)` mutates the input.
Complexity: O(n log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space excluding sorting.
complexity_reason: The two smallest values are included as a candidate because their product may be positive and exceed the product of the three largest.

notes:
Task and constraints: `averageOfLevels(root)` returns the arithmetic mean of node values at each binary-tree depth from top to bottom.
Idea: Return an empty list for a null root; otherwise use `deque` breadth-first traversal and process a fixed `size` number of nodes per level.
Technique and why it applies: `size = len(q)` snapshots the current level, `total` accumulates its values, and child nodes are appended for the next level before `total / size` is added to `out`.
Invariant: At the start of each outer loop, `q` contains exactly the nodes at one depth; each is removed once and its children form later levels.
Edge cases: Null root returns `[]`; a single-node tree returns its value as a floating-point average; `size` is positive whenever the loop runs.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(w) queue space for maximum tree width w.
complexity_reason: Capturing `size` before the inner loop prevents children added during traversal from being included in their parent's level average.

notes:
Task and constraints: `averageOfLevels(TreeNode root)` returns one average per level of a binary tree.
Idea: Use a `Queue<TreeNode>` for breadth-first traversal, snapshot its size for each level, and accumulate node values in `double sum`.
Technique and why it applies: The inner loop runs `size` times, removes nodes with `q.remove()`, enqueues non-null children, then appends `sum / size` to `out`.
Invariant: Each outer iteration processes exactly the nodes that were in the queue at the start of that level, so newly enqueued children belong to the next average.
Edge cases: A null root returns an empty list; a single root yields one average; `ArrayDeque` is safe because null children are checked before enqueueing.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(w) queue space for maximum level width w.
complexity_reason: The saved queue size separates the current level from children enqueued while processing that level.

notes:
Task and constraints: `findMaxAverage(nums, k)` finds the maximum average among all contiguous windows of exactly `k` elements.
Idea: Sum the initial window, then slide it one position at a time while tracking `total` and the largest sum `best`.
Technique and why it applies: Each update adds `nums[i]` and subtracts the departing `nums[i-k]`, reusing the previous window sum instead of summing each window again.
Invariant: Before each comparison, `total` is the sum of the length-`k` window ending at index `i`, and `best` is the largest sum seen.
Edge cases: `k` must be positive and no greater than the list length; negative values are handled because all fixed-length windows are compared.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The entering and leaving elements update the sum in constant time, so the algorithm avoids rescanning each window.

notes:
Task and constraints: `findMaxAverage(int[] a, int k)` returns the maximum average of any contiguous subarray of length `k`.
Idea: Compute the first `k`-element `sum`, store it as `best`, then slide the window across the rest of `a`.
Technique and why it applies: `sum += a[i] - a[i-k]` adds the incoming value and removes the outgoing one; `(double) best / k` ensures floating-point division in the return value.
Invariant: After each slide, `sum` represents exactly one window of length `k`, and `best` stores the maximum window sum encountered.
Edge cases: `k` must be between one and the array length; negative entries do not affect correctness because every window has equal size.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Casting `best` to double before division prevents integer truncation of the average.

notes:
Task and constraints: `findErrorNums(nums)` returns the duplicated value and the missing value from an array expected to contain every integer from one through its length.
Idea: Track seen values in `seen`, remember the repeated number in `duplicate`, then find the first absent integer in the required range.
Technique and why it applies: Membership in `seen` identifies a duplicate; `next(x for x in range(1, len(nums)+1) if x not in seen)` finds the missing value.
Invariant: After each input value, `seen` contains all values processed so far, and `duplicate` records the value encountered more than once.
Edge cases: The input guarantee supplies one duplicate and one missing value; the method relies on values being in the range 1 through n and mutates no input data.
Complexity: O(n) expected time and O(n) auxiliary space for the set.
complexity_reason: The value range guarantees exactly one absent number, and `seen` makes its search a linear expected-time membership scan.

notes:
Task and constraints: `findErrorNums(int[] a)` identifies the repeated value and the missing value in an array intended to contain 1 through n.
Idea: Use a boolean `seen` array indexed by value, detect the duplicate during the first pass, then scan for the first false entry.
Technique and why it applies: `seen[x]` records whether x has appeared; a second occurrence sets `dup`, and the final loop returns `{dup, x}` for the first unseen value.
Invariant: After processing each input item, `seen[v]` is true exactly when value v has appeared, and `dup` stores the repeated value once detected.
Edge cases: The input is assumed to contain values within 1 through n and exactly one duplicate/missing pair; the fallback empty array is unreachable under those guarantees.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space for the boolean array.
complexity_reason: The index-aligned boolean array makes both duplicate detection and missing-value discovery direct linear scans.
